title: AI Implementation Guide: Use Cases, Evaluation, and Risk Controls
description: A practical framework for introducing AI at work: choose a bounded use case, evaluate quality and risk, protect data, measure outcomes, and plan human oversight.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Choose a Narrow, Measurable Use Case
sections.body: Begin with one repeatable task where the inputs, expected output, and consequences of error can be described. Good pilot candidates often assist an existing workflow—drafting an internal summary, classifying support requests, extracting fields for review, or searching approved documentation—rather than making consequential decisions without oversight. Record the current baseline: time per task, rework rate, quality criteria, volume, and who is accountable. Define what the system must never do, such as send customer messages or change records without approval. If the task has no clear owner or measurable problem, pause before choosing a model.

sections.title: Map Data and Access Before Selecting a Model
sections.body: List the information the workflow needs, where it comes from, who is permitted to see it, and whether it contains personal, confidential, regulated, or customer data. Minimize inputs and use synthetic or redacted examples during early testing. Review the provider's current retention, training-use, deletion, access-control, regional-processing, and contractual terms rather than assuming all plans behave alike. Separate public information from internal knowledge, restrict connectors to the smallest useful scope, and create a process to revoke access. Involve security, privacy, legal, or compliance owners when the use case warrants it.

sections.title: Evaluate Quality With a Representative Test Set
sections.body: Build a small test set that reflects ordinary cases, difficult edge cases, ambiguous requests, and examples where the correct response is to refuse or ask for clarification. Have a qualified reviewer define acceptable outputs before comparing systems. Score factual correctness, completeness, consistency, latency, usability, and the amount of human correction required. Keep the prompts, model version, settings, test examples, and results together so the evaluation can be repeated. Do not use a few impressive demonstrations as evidence that a system is reliable across the full workflow.

sections.title: Design Human Review and Failure Handling
sections.body: Decide which outputs can be used automatically, which require approval, and which must be escalated. For high-impact or customer-facing work, make the review step visible and give reviewers enough context to verify claims against trusted sources. Provide a fallback path when the model is unavailable, uncertain, or produces malformed output. Log material errors without collecting more sensitive data than necessary, define who can stop the workflow, and test how users report failures. Human review is only a control if reviewers have time, authority, and clear criteria—not merely a button to approve everything.

sections.title: Integrate in Small, Reversible Steps
sections.body: Start with a sandbox or shadow mode in which outputs are compared with the existing process but do not change live records. Then enable a limited pilot for a named group, with rate limits, access restrictions, monitoring, and a rollback plan. Test prompt injection, misleading retrieved documents, data leakage, unauthorized actions, and unexpected tool calls where relevant. Keep secrets out of prompts and client-side code. Version prompts and configuration like other production changes, and review dependencies whenever the provider, model, retrieval index, or connected system changes.

sections.title: Measure Value Without Inflated ROI Claims
sections.body: Compare pilot results with the baseline using the same task definition and quality bar. Track completion time, accepted-output rate, correction time, error severity, user adoption, operating cost, and downstream effects. Include implementation, integration, review, monitoring, and training costs rather than counting only model usage. Separate observed results from estimates, report sample size and measurement period, and note any seasonal or workflow changes. Do not assume time saved becomes cash savings unless staffing or capacity actually changes. Expand only when quality and risk controls remain acceptable at realistic volume.

sections.title: Govern, Monitor, and Reassess
sections.body: Assign an accountable owner for the use case, data, evaluation, incidents, and ongoing cost. Document intended use, prohibited use, known limitations, model/provider details, review requirements, and a contact for incidents. Monitor drift in input patterns, failure rates, user overrides, and cost; periodically rerun the test set and review access permissions. Keep a human-readable change log and a retirement plan for when performance declines or the business need disappears. A successful pilot is not a permanent approval: reassess after material model, data, integration, policy, or workflow changes.
